# Isaiah 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## Overview of the Chapter

Isaiah 22 contains two oracles: (1) vv. 1–14, a judgment against Jerusalem ("the Valley of Vision") for self-sufficiency and refusal to repent under threat of siege; and (2) vv. 15–25, concerning the deposition of the proud steward Shebna and the elevation of Eliakim, who serves as a type of Christ. Most traditional commentators identify the historical setting as Sennacherib's invasion of Judah in 701 BC, with the preparations described matching those of Hezekiah in 2 Chronicles 32:2–5.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

---

## Part One: Judgment on Jerusalem (vv. 1–14)

### v. 1 — "This is the burden against the Valley of Vision: What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the rooftops…"

**"Valley of Vision"** is an enigmatic title for Jerusalem. Jerusalem sits on a hill but is surrounded by higher hills and three valleys (Kidron, Hinnom, Tyropoeon), so it appears as if in a valley. It is called "of vision" because it was the seat of prophecy and the dwelling-place of the prophets, including Isaiah himself. Gill notes the Septuagint renders it "the valley of Sion." The Pulpit Commentary explains that from Isaiah's house in the lower city, Jerusalem would appear in a valley relative to the surrounding mountains. Delitzsch, cited by the Pulpit Commentary, notes that the city is "the inhabitant of the valley" compared to the mountains (Jeremiah 21:13).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

**"Gone up to the rooftops"** — Flat roofs were places of public concourse, observation, and celebration (Judges 16:27; Nehemiah 8:16). Gill says they went up either for safety from the enemy, to observe enemy movements, to cast arrows down, or to mourn and cry to heaven. The Pulpit Commentary adds that they went up for feasting and revelry. Ellicott sees the people in a state of excitement, keeping their revels with reckless despair.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 2 — "O city of commotion, O town of revelry? Your slain did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle."

Jerusalem was formerly full of noise, commerce, and rejoicing. Gill notes the city was "full of stirs" — through the multitude of people and business — but now is hushed and quiet. The "slain" died not by the sword but by famine or pestilence during the siege — an inglorious kind of death. Poole (cited by Guzik) says they died "either by famine or pestilence in the siege, as many died, Jeremiah 14:18, 38:2, or in their flight." Sennacherib's own inscription says: "Hezekiah, like a caged bird, within Jerusalem, his royal city, I confined."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 3 — "All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow…"

Ellicott reads this as a taunting charge of cowardice: the rulers ventured on a sortie and were captured without even drawing their bows. The Pulpit Commentary says numbers of the principal men, regarding resistance as vain, tried to escape the doomed town but were captured and bound by the enemy's archers — "all bound together," as captives bound by a single rope in Egyptian bas-reliefs. Gill adds that they were so panicked they had no strength to draw the bow.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 4 — "Therefore I said, 'Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.'"

Isaiah turns from describing the scene to his own grief. He wishes to be alone with his sorrow and refuses all consolation. Guzik notes that while Jeremiah is known as the "weeping prophet," Isaiah also wept bitterly when he saw judgment coming against God's people. Ellicott compares Isaiah's lament to Jeremiah's over a later catastrophe (Lamentations 3:48). Gill says the prophet speaks to those around him: "Look away from me, turn away from me… leave me to myself, that I may weep in secret."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 5 — "For the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision—of breaking down the walls and crying to the mountains."

The calamity is not mere chance; it is a day appointed by the Lord GOD of Hosts. The Pulpit Commentary renders it: "the Lord has a day" — God has such a day in reserve. "Breaking down the walls" likely refers to undermining, a practice shown in Assyrian sculptures using swords, spears, crowbars, or axes to dislodge stones. Some modern scholars (Ewald, Cheyne, cited by the Pulpit Commentary) read "Kir" and "Shoa" as proper names in this verse rather than "walls" and "crying," but the traditional reading is preferred.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 6 — "Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield."

Elam (the Persians) and Kir (the Medes or a region in Mesopotamia) are named as elements of the Assyrian invading army. Elam was famous for its archers (Jeremiah 49:35). Gill says the Elamites, though normally hostile to Assyria, were at this time subject to the Assyrians and served in Sennacherib's army. "Kir uncovered the shield" means they drew the shield from its leather case to prepare for battle (Ellicott, citing Caesar's *Bellum Gallicum* 2:21 for the parallel practice).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 7 — "Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates."

The valleys around Jerusalem — Gibeon, Rephaim, Hinnom, Jehoshaphat — which were once filled with choice crops or vines, are now filled with enemy chariots. The horsemen array themselves at the very gate of the city, ready to force entry.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 8 — "He has uncovered the defenses of Judah. On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest."

**"He"** — Ellicott says Jehovah removed the veil that had hidden the approaching danger from the inhabitants and laid bare their weakness. The Pulpit Commentary says the "covering of Judah" was what hid their weakness from themselves; God drew it aside, and they suddenly saw their danger. Gill says it was the enemy (Sennacherib) who uncovered Judah's defences by taking the fenced cities (2 Kings 18:13).

**"House of the Forest"** — the "House of the Forest of Lebanon" (1 Kings 7:2-5), built by Solomon, which served as an armoury containing shields and weapons (1 Kings 10:17).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/

### v. 9 — "You saw that there were many breaches in the walls of the City of David. You collected water from the lower pool."

The "City of David" refers either to Jerusalem generally or specifically to the fortress of Zion (the eastern hill). Hezekiah repaired these breaches (2 Chronicles 32:5). The Pulpit Commentary gives a detailed account of Hezekiah's water-works: he covered the open upper pool to deny water to the Assyrians, made an underground conduit within the city, and may have cut the Siloam tunnel to convey water from the Gihon spring. "You collected water from the lower pool" — the Lower Gihon (now Birket-es-Sultan) — was gathered to supply the city during siege and to deprive the enemy.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 10 — "You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall."

The houses were numbered to determine which could be pulled down for materials to repair and strengthen the walls — a sign of extreme haste and urgency. Gill gives several possibilities: to know how many men were available for military duty, to levy taxes for defence, to assess provisions, or most likely, to see which houses could be torn down to use their stones and timber for fortifying the wall.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 11 — "You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago."

This is the theological heart of the first oracle. Ellicott identifies the "ditch" (reservoir) as probably the "pool of Hezekiah" (Birket-el-Batrak), between two walls north of Zion. The "old pool" was likely the pool of Siloam or the king's pool (Nehemiah 2:14).

But the key complaint is: they looked to their physical defences and water-works but **not to the Maker**. Guzik says: "All their care in defending the city would not matter because God had removed the protection of Judah.… The best thing Jerusalem could do for her protection was to turn her heart toward the LORD." The Pulpit Commentary says: "Ye have not looked unto the maker thereof" means you have not looked to God, who in His eternal counsels foreknew and decreed all these steps. Delitzsch (cited in Pulpit Homiletics) adds that Jerusalem might have averted the fate "if Jerusalem repented, that realization would be averted."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

### v. 12 — "On that day the Lord GOD of Hosts called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth."

The Lord's call was to repentance, expressed outwardly in weeping, shaving the head (a natural sign of grief, not the forbidden pagan practice, per the Pulpit Commentary), and wearing sackcloth. This was the proper response to national danger — like the fast described in Joel 2. The call came through the voice of Providence (the siege itself) and through the prophets.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 13 — "But look, there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!'"

Instead of repentance, the people chose reckless feasting. Guzik says they had "both confidence in their own preparation (joy and gladness) and a fatalistic outlook toward the future." Ellicott compares this to the plague at Athens under Pericles and the plague of Florence in Boccaccio's time — danger leading not to repentance but to sensuality. The Pulpit Commentary notes that "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" is a universal sentiment of despair, similar to the supposed epitaph of Sardanapalus. The Apostle Paul quotes this phrase in 1 Corinthians 15:32 in the context of the resurrection — if there is no resurrection, this is the only logical way to live.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 14 — "The LORD of Hosts has revealed in my hearing: 'Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for,' says the Lord GOD of Hosts."

This is one of the most sobering verses in Isaiah. The sin is specifically the refusal to humble oneself before the Lord and repent. Guzik says: "Jerusalem was doing everything except the essential thing." The Pulpit Commentary states: "The sin of turning a call to repentance into an excuse for rioting and drunkenness is one which God will not pardon. It implies a hardness of heart which cannot fail to issue in final impenitence."

Dr. Constable (from search excerpts) notes: "Unbelief persisted in until death is the only sin that God will not forgive.… Repentance was still possible for Isaiah's original audience when he gave this message. The warning passages in Hebrews explain that a time can come when people are no longer able to repent."

Gill notes the Targum renders it: "the prophet said, with mine ears I was hearing, when this was decreed from before the Lord of hosts." This was a divine oracle revealed inwardly to Isaiah.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm

---

## Part Two: Shebna and Eliakim (vv. 15–25)

### v. 15 — "This is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: 'Go, say to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace…'"

Shebna is a historical figure, a high official under King Hezekiah. He appears in 2 Kings 18:18 and Isaiah 36:3 as "the scribe" and was formerly "over the house" — the highest office a subject could hold, akin to a vizier, prime minister, or "mayor of the palace." Ellicott notes the word for "treasurer" (literally "companion") implies a position like that of the "king's friend" (Genesis 26:26; 2 Samuel 15:37). The Pulpit Commentary says "this" is contemptuous — "this Shebna" — and suggests the name is Syriac rather than Hebrew, making Shebna possibly a foreign adventurer, perhaps a refugee from Damascus.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/

### v. 16 — "What are you doing here, and who authorized you to carve out a tomb for yourself here—to chisel your tomb in the height and cut your resting place in the rock?"

Shebna's pride is exposed in his elaborate, elevated rock-hewn tomb. Since he apparently had no ancestral connections in Jerusalem (the questions "What have you here, and whom have you here?" imply he was a foreigner), his grand sepulchre was pure self-glorification. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Jewish tombs of any pretension were excavations in solid rock on hillsides. Guzik observes that Shebna built his tomb as if to say: "I will never be carried away in exile. I am so certain that I will die here that I will build my tomb here" — directly contradicting Isaiah's prophecies of exile. Archaeologists have found remains of a grave hewn by one Shebna on the Mount of Olives (noted by Dr. Constable).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

### vv. 17–18 — "Look, O mighty man! The LORD is about to shake you violently. He will take hold of you, roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land…"

The language is vivid and almost violent. Ellicott renders v. 17: "will hurl thee with the hurling of a mighty man." For v. 18, the picture is of a ball flung violently onto a smooth plain where it bounces on and on with nothing to stop it. The "large country" is probably the plain of Mesopotamia. His "glorious chariots" — another display of his ostentatious pride — will become the shame of his master's house. Ellicott notes that chariots were normally used only by kings; Shebna had appeared in stately chariots like those of royalty.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 19 — "I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position."

God Himself declares Shebna's deposition. When we next meet Shebna in Isaiah 36:22, he occupies the inferior position of "scribe," while Eliakim has taken his place as "over the household." The prophecy was fulfilled partially in this demotion; whether Shebna later died in exile is not recorded in Scripture. The Pulpit Commentary suggests he may have fled to Egypt.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/

### v. 20 — "On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah."

Eliakim is called "My servant" — a title of high honour when given by God Himself (used also of David, Moses, and the Messiah). Nothing is known of Eliakim's previous history, but the epithet testifies to his faith. Ellicott suggests he was probably, in heart if not openly, one of Isaiah's disciples.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/

### v. 21 — "I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him. I will put your authority in his hand, and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah."

A literal investiture: Shebna's robe and sash — the insignia of his office — would be transferred to Eliakim. "He shall be a father" means a protector, counsellor, and guide (cf. Job 29:16). The Pulpit Commentary notes it is perhaps implied that Shebna had not conducted himself as a "father."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

### v. 22 — "I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open."

**This verse is of major Christological significance.** The key was the special badge of the chief steward's office, symbolising control over the king's treasure-chambers and the gates of the palace. Ellicott notes it was solemnly laid on the shoulder of the new official, perhaps representing the burden of responsibility. The steward alone decided who was admitted to the king's presence and who received from the king's treasury.

**Christological application:** Jesus directly applies this language to Himself in Revelation 3:7: "He who has the key of David, He who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens." Guzik writes: "Jesus is the one with the keys of Hades and of Death (Revelation 1:18), who has all authority both in heaven and on earth. Jesus delegates this authority as it pleases Him (Matthew 16:19)." The Pulpit Commentary also notes that the reference in Revelation 3:7 is sufficient to show that Eliakim is, to a certain extent, a type of Christ.

Guzik adds: "Eliakim, barely mentioned elsewhere in Scripture, becomes 'famous in heaven' because his heart is turned toward the Lord, not toward selfish ambition like Shebna's."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

### v. 23 — "I will drive him like a peg into a firm place, and he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father."

The "nail" or "peg" is a symbol of secure support. Ellicott explains it is a peg driven into a wall (as in Ezekiel 15:3), not a tent-peg. In ancient homes, items were stored by hanging them on pegs set around the room. If something was on its peg, it was safe and secure. The "throne of glory" is another symbol of sovereignty and honour that Eliakim will bring to his previously obscure family.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 24 — "So they will hang on him all the glory of his father's house: the descendants and the offshoots—all the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar."

The metaphor of the peg continues. All Eliakim's relatives — the "glory" (or "weight," the Hebrew has both meanings) of his family, both prominent descendants and obscure offshoots — will depend on him. The "vessels" (cups to flagons) represent all the retainers, from the most honoured to the least, who will "hang" on his support.

Ellicott detects a note of irony: there is the danger even for Eliakim, upright as he is, of giving way to nepotism — and the fault would not remain unpunished (see v. 25). Guzik applies this to Christ: "There are many different vessels in the LORD's house, with many different sizes and purposes. But they all must hang on the same peg! All will be equally wrecked if they drop from the peg. The safety isn't in the size or quality of the vessel, but in its attachment to the peg."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

### v. 25 — "In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall, and the load upon it will be cut down. Indeed, the LORD has spoken."

This final verse introduces a twist. Two main interpretations exist among the commentators:

**Interpretation 1 — Shebna as the peg:** Guzik argues that if Eliakim is yet to be promoted (v. 23, "I will fasten him as a peg"), then Shebna is the peg currently fastened. Therefore, before Eliakim can be put in his rightful place, Shebna must be "removed and be cut down and fall." The burden on him (all who relied on him) will be cut off. Guzik says: "When Shebna was removed, all those who 'hung' on him were also cut off. We have to make sure that we are resting on the right 'peg.'"

**Interpretation 2 — Eliakim as the peg (and a warning):** Ellicott says there is a judgment even for the misuse of power portrayed in v. 24. The "nail" that seems so firmly fixed shall be removed — i.e., Eliakim shall cease to hold his high office, and with his fall comes that of all his kindred and dependents. The Pulpit Commentary similarly sees this as a warning that even Eliakim, good as he is, is not the ultimate peg; only the Messiah can bear the full weight.

Dr. Constable (from search excerpts) says: "Unfortunately, Eliakim would not be able to carry all the weight of responsibility committed to him and would fail. Thus the people's trust in another human being, even a very capable person, would prove misplaced. They could only safely trust in the Lord Almighty."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

---

## Denominational and Theological Distinctives

### Reformed / Presbyterian

No distinctively Reformed commentary on Isaiah 22 from Ligonier or monergism.com was located in the available searches. However, Calvin's approach (cited second-hand by the Pulpit Homiletics) emphasises that ministers ought to groan when they perceive the tokens of approaching ruin, reflecting the Reformed emphasis on God's sovereignty over judgment. The Reformed reading would stress that God Himself "removed the protection of Judah" (v. 8) — judgment comes from His hand, not merely from human armies.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/isaiah/22.htm

### Baptist

John Gill (a Reformed Baptist) holds that the invasion was by the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, not the Babylonians. His approach is strongly historical-grammatical, and he identifies Elamites and Medes specifically as serving in the Assyrian forces. Gill also emphasises that v. 14 speaks of a judgment of hardness — the sin of scoffing at God's warnings.

No distinctively Baptist material from Spurgeon or Desiring God on this specific chapter was found in the searches. John Piper (Desiring God) has messages on other Isaiah passages (chs. 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 26, 40, 43) but not specifically on Isaiah 22.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/22.htm
- https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/isaiah/messages

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

David Guzik (Enduring Word) provides the most thorough verse-by-verse treatment found. His distinctives include: (a) a strong Christological typology — Eliakim as a clear type of Christ who holds the keys; (b) pastoral application throughout, e.g., "We need to accept both the open and the shut doors" that Jesus places in our lives; (c) an emphasis on self-examination — "We have to make sure we are resting on the right peg."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-22/

### Anglican

Charles Ellicott's commentary (Anglican) is notable for its careful historical detail, linguistic notes, and classical parallels (e.g., comparing the uncovering of shields to Caesar's *Gallic Wars*, and the "eat and drink" ethos to the plague at Athens). Ellicott also provides nuance on the peg imagery, seeing it as both a promise and a warning about the misuse of power.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/22.htm

### Evangelical (Dallas Seminary / Dispensational)

Dr. Thomas Constable's notes (from search excerpts) approach the chapter through the theme of self-sufficiency versus trust in God. He treats the three sections (Jerusalem, Shebna, Eliakim) as revealing the thoroughness of Israel's sin of seeking security in the world. Notably, Constable holds that Eliakim himself would eventually fail (v. 25), making the ultimate point that only the Lord Almighty can be trusted without disappointment.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-22.html

### Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox

No distinctively Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), or Orthodox (oca.org) material on Isaiah 22 was located in the available searches.

### Modern Scholarship

The available searches did not locate specific material from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org notes on Isaiah 22. However, some modern critical views are noted by the Pulpit Commentary: scholars like Ewald, Cheyne, and Luzzatto read v. 5 differently, treating "Kir" and "Shoa" as proper names of nations involved in undermining and attacking, rather than "walls" and "crying." The Pulpit Commentary rejects this reading.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/22.htm

---

## Key Themes and Applications Across Traditions

1. **Self-sufficiency versus trust in God** — the central sin of Jerusalem was doing everything *except* turning to the Lord (v. 11). This is the unifying theme across all commentators consulted.

2. **The unforgivable sin of unrepentant hardness** (v. 14) — all traditions agree that the sin with "no atonement" is the persistent refusal to humble oneself before God.

3. **Eliakim as a type of Christ** (v. 22) — universally recognised across traditions, anchored by Revelation 3:7.

4. **The danger of misplaced trust** — whether in walls, water systems, capable leaders, or even godly men like Eliakim — the peg will eventually give way if it is not Christ Himself.
